items.title: [django-filer] django-filer: Missing per-object authorization on `discard` and `edit_redirect` version transitions
items.summary: SummaryWhen django-filer's optional per-folder permission system is enabled (FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS=True), the "Delete files and/or folders" admin action does not enforce per-folder edit permissions the way every other mutating action does. A staff user who is scoped read-only on a folder via FolderPermission (can_edit = DENY), but who holds the global Django model-level delete_* permission, can delete files and entire subfolders inside that folder — even though their move, rename, copy, and resize actions on the same folder are correctly denied.This is an integrity / edit-control gap (unauthorized deletion). It is not a read-confidentiality issue: filer files are world-downloadable by design, so no confidentiality claim is made.Affected versionsdjango-filer <= 3.4.4 (verified end-to-end on 3.4.4 and on master prior to   the fix).Only installations running with FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS = True (the optional per-folder FolderPermission system) are affected. Deployments that leave permissions disabled (the default) rely solely on Django model-level permissions and are not impacted by this specific gap.Patched versionsFixed in PR #1605.   Upgrade to the first release containing that commit (3.5.0 or later).DetailsThe delete_files_or_folders admin action in filer/admin/folderadmin.py authorized deletion using only:self.has_delete_permission(request) — which returns True for obj=None, andthe Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image    permission (enforced downstream by the admin delete machinery).It never called check_folder_edit_permissions or check_files_edit_permissions. Every sibling mutating action — move, rename, copy, resize — does call these helpers, which walk the selected objects (and their descendants) and enforce the per-folder can_edit grant from FolderPermission.Because FolderPermission has no dedicated can_delete field, deletion is treated as an edit/management operation and is gated elsewhere on can_edit. The delete action's omission therefore let a folder-scoped read-only user bypass the per-folder control that constrains all their other write operations.PreconditionThe attacker must hold the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission. A purely read-only user (no model-level delete perm) receives 403 and cannot exploit this. This precondition matches the standard folder-scoped-staff deployment model, where staff hold model-level permissions and are further constrained per-folder by FolderPermission. MitigationUpgrade to the patched release.Until upgrading, avoid granting the model-level delete_file /delete_folder / delete_image permission to staff who are meant to beread-only on specific folders via FolderPermission.CreditReported through coordinated disclosure. Fixed in PR #1605.Referenceshttps://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/security/advisories/GHSA-vf85-8ff2-3r9whttps://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/pull/1605https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/commit/29d20ec0de13d7f77fa2cea93166f8d50a3f508dhttps://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/commit/742ba4c3094dd75e586ca3a05e6ad2703de4553bhttps://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/releases/tag/3.5.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf85-8ff2-3r9w

items.title: [djangocms-versioning] djangocms-versioning: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key and Missing Authorization
items.summary: SummaryThe discard and edit_redirect version transitions did not enforce a per-object change-permission check, while the sibling transitions (archive, publish, unpublish, revert) all did. As a result a low-privileged staff user could discard (delete) any draft version — and thereby the underlying content object — of content they have no change permission on, and could create an editable draft off any published version, by supplying a version primary key they should not have access to (an insecure direct object reference).DetailsVersion state transitions are guarded by Conditions objects declared on djangocms_versioning.models.Version. Every transition that mutates content carries the user_can_change condition, which delegates to the content object's own permission check (Version.has_change_permission → content.has_change_permission / has_placeholder_change_permission, with a final fallback to the Django change_<model> permission).Two conditions were missing that check:# Before (vulnerable)check_discard = Conditions([    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),])check_edit_redirect = Conditions([    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),])The corresponding admin views authorize only through these conditions:VersionAdmin.discard_view / VersionAdmin.edit_redirect_view fetch the  target with the stock ModelAdmin.get_object, which is backed by the   unfiltered default queryset — no per-user or per-grouper scoping.The views are registered with admin_site.admin_view, which enforces only  is_staff.discard_view deletes the version directly via version.delete() and   never consults VersionAdmin.has_delete_permission (which otherwise   delegates to the content admin and honors ALLOW_DELETING_VERSIONS).Because the only per-object gate for these two operations was the Conditions list, and that list omitted user_can_change, any staff user could invoke the operation on any version by its primary key. The changelist action buttons are disabled in the UI via check_discard.as_bool / check_edit_redirect.as_bool, but that is a client-side affordance only and does not protect the directly reachable admin URLs.ImpactType: Broken access control / missing authorization (IDOR).Who is affected: Multi-editor deployments where staff users hold  differentiated per-object permissions.Under CMS_PERMISSION = True, authorization for these two operations was   effectively reduced to is_staff, so any staff user could discard or    edit-redirect any version.Under the default CMS_PERMISSION = False, it degrades to the global    change_<model> permission (e.g. cms.change_page) — weaker than the  intended per-object check, but not absent.Consequence: Unauthorized deletion of draft versions and their content objects (integrity/availability of content), and unauthorized creation of drafts from published content.PatchesFixed by adding the user_can_change condition to both check_discard and check_edit_redirect, restoring parity with the other content-mutating transitions:# After (fixed)check_discard = Conditions([    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),    user_can_change(change_permission_error),    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),])check_edit_redirect = Conditions([    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),    user_can_change(change_permission_error),    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),])discard intentionally requires change permission (not delete): it is treated as undoing changes to a draft.Upgrade to djangocms-versioning 2.6.1 or later.WorkaroundsThere is no configuration-only workaround. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately should restrict staff accounts to trusted users, since the missing gate reduces to is_staff under CMS_PERMISSION = True.Referenceshttps://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/security/advisories/GHSA-5g9x-qwh5-33x4https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/pull/573https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/commit/d8c570daa5f7805e8be51f15545fe77b24c44dafhttps://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/releases/tag/2.6.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g9x-qwh5-33x4
